In a semi-arid interior basin, two remaining large tracts of native bunchgrass prairie are separated by a three-kilometre belt of irrigated forage-seed fields. The belt is the only area with the soil depth, slope, and elevation needed to restore the same prairie community between them. If a regional planning commission acquires the fields at market value, retires irrigation, removes leveling berms, restores natural microtopography, and seeds native grasses and forbs, a broad functional prairie belt will develop over roughly ten to fifteen years. It will provide cover, feeding sites, and breeding habitat for movement-limited grassland insects and small reptiles, allowing repeated movement, recolonization, and plant dispersal between the remnants. Keeping the fields in production leaves the remnants isolated by frequently cut crops, pesticide exposure, and bare service lanes.

The commission may instead retain the agricultural designation. That would preserve enough forage-seed acreage for the local cleaning plant to meet its minimum operating threshold, sustaining growers’ nearby processing, contractors’ work, employment, and retail demand in the service town. Although landowners would receive market-value payments if the fields were acquired, restoration would reduce seed volume below the plant’s threshold. The plant is expected to close, contractors would lose work, and seasonal and permanent earnings and commercial activity would decline persistently. Should the regional planning commission choose habitat restoration that reconnects the prairie remnants or retain irrigated seed production to protect local economic stability?

In an Arctic archipelago, a storm has damaged the sheltered inlet harbor that supplies several remote settlements with fuel for household heating and diesel-generated electricity. The national government owns an adjacent raised beach containing the only aggregate tested as suitable and available in sufficient volume to rebuild the harbor for full-size seasonal fuel vessels. It can designate the parcel a no-quarry, no-industrial-use conservation zone or authorize quarrying and reconstruction.

Conservation would leave the inlet’s water exchange intact and prevent sediment from entering its shallows. Its kelp forests, capelin spawning grounds, soft-bottom benthic communities, seabird feeding areas, and seals would remain connected in their present functioning condition. If quarrying and the required breakwater proceed, fine sediment would settle on kelp holdfasts and capelin spawning substrate, while the narrowed inlet would retain more suspended material. Kelp and spawning habitat would contract, and the inlet would shift toward a less diverse, silt-tolerant benthic community with less prey support for fish, seabirds, and seals.

Without the full-size harbor, fuel must arrive by repeated small-barge shipments during a short calm-weather season. Heating and electricity prices would rise substantially, households and businesses would face fuel allocations, and nonessential commercial power would sometimes be cut. Minimum household heating and essential services would remain protected. Rebuilding the harbor would restore predictable fuel inventories, lower energy costs, and avoid routine limits. Should the national government choose the conservation zone that protects the marine ecosystem or authorize the quarry and harbor works that protect reliable energy access?

A public land-management authority controls the groundwater wells, spring-flow rights, bypass gates, and canal headworks serving a desert spring complex and nearby family-owned date groves. Four linked spring channels support an endemic hydrobiid snail found nowhere else. In critically dry years, reserving the first 1.8 million litres per day for the springs during the hottest eight weeks would keep every channel flowing, oxygenated, and below the snail’s lethal temperature boundary. The snail would continue to breed throughout its entire range and disperse among channels, preserving the biological distinctiveness of the spring complex.

That reservation would reduce irrigation deliveries to the groves. Roughly one-third of orchard acreage would experience persistently lower yields, and repeated dry-year reductions would shorten the productive lives of mature palms on that land. The owners would retain their homes, most production, and viable businesses, but would lose substantial crop income and capital value in long-established private orchards. If the authority instead provides full established dry-season deliveries, all mature palms can be maintained, preserving crop production, orchard longevity, and ordinary agricultural and market value. But the two lowest spring channels would become warm, stagnant pools, their snail populations would be lost, and the species’ occupied range would be reduced by about half.

Should the public land-management authority reserve water to protect the endemic snail across all four channels, or provide full deliveries to protect the date-grove owners’ established property use?

A century-old tidal dam encloses Heron Polder, where 64 lawful homes stand within the natural tidal frame. By excluding ordinary high tides, the barrier has turned a former estuary into a shallow freshwater impoundment dominated by limited freshwater plants and small fish. Marine nursery access, tidally renewed benthic prey, and regular feeding by larger estuarine fish and shorebirds are absent. If the dam is completely removed, twice-daily saline inundation and sediment exchange will restore salt-marsh vegetation, benthic invertebrates, juvenile-fish nursery use, and feeding access for larger fish and fish-eating birds, reestablishing a connected estuarine food web across the polder and adjacent bay.

Removal would also bring ordinary tides onto village roads, utilities, sewer infrastructure, and house floors, making permanent occupancy impossible. The environmental regulatory agency can require relocation before breaching, with acquisition, replacement housing, tenant protections, moving assistance, and reconstructed community facilities in a nearby purpose-built neighborhood on higher ground. Yet residents would permanently lose their current homes, historic village site, familiar landscape, and exact place-based relationships. Renewing and rehabilitating the dam would allow them to remain safely in their homes and preserve their daily-support networks, but the estuarine food web would not return. Gate schedules, a ring levee, and elevating homes cannot both protect present residence and substantially restore the food web. Should the environmental regulatory agency remove the dam to protect trophic integrity or renew it to protect residents’ continued residence?

A municipal council must decide the future of a low floodplain where community allotments occupy the narrow strip between two remnant oxbow wetlands. Drainage ditches and low berms allow cultivation but keep this only restorable connection dry, interrupting movement of water, sediment, organic matter, seeds, amphibians, and aquatic invertebrates. Monitoring shows that the smaller wetland’s shallow-water vegetation and amphibian occupancy are declining as its populations remain isolated. If the council designates the floodplain as a protected area, ends the licenses after notice, removes berms, and plugs the ditches, seasonal flows will reconnect the oxbows. The basins will again function as a continuous wetland complex with a broader range of characteristic habitats and communities.

The allotments, however, provide low-income residents in nearby apartment blocks with a substantial share of their fresh vegetables, and surplus is exchanged with neighbors. If cultivation ends, compensation will cover tools and approved improvements but not recurring harvests. Gardeners will have to buy higher-priced produce from nearby shops or take a long bus trip to a discount market, reducing the variety and regularity of fresh vegetables and making familiar crops harder to obtain. Staple foods will remain available. Renewing the licenses would preserve this nearby, inexpensive food source, but ditch clearing and cultivation would maintain the ecological break.

Should the municipal council designate the protected area to restore wetland continuity or renew the allotment licenses to protect residents’ food access?

A state natural-resources agency must decide whether to permit annual basin-wide systemic herbicide treatment in a state-owned reservoir’s only sheltered sailing and paddling basin. Dense hydrilla mats have spread through the launch lanes, instruction circuit, and assisted capsize-recovery area, making them unusable. Treatment at the concentration and duration supported by agency trials would suppress hydrilla enough to keep the basin navigable for sailing instruction, adaptive paddling, recovery practice, and regular small-craft recreation. The reservoir’s other arms have stronger wind, wakes, and motor traffic and cannot provide equivalent conditions; without treatment, hydrilla will again cover the usable basin within two growing seasons, ending these programs and regular use of the sheltered water.

Yet hydrilla is interwoven with native pondweed that includes distinct warm-shoal and deep-water ecotypes. Several heat- and depth-associated alleles are concentrated in the warm-shoal plants. Repeated systemic-herbicide exposure would eliminate most flowering warm-shoal plants and sharply reduce their recruitment. Although deep-water pondweed would remain, the reservoir would lose the ecotype holding most of its warm-shoal and heat-associated alleles. Prohibiting treatment would preserve viable breeding stands across the depth gradient, along with their differentiated alleles and continuing gene exchange. Agency trials and site constraints have ruled out lower-dose, mechanical, spatial, and relocation alternatives that would avoid these consequences.

Should the agency prohibit systemic herbicide treatment to protect the pondweed’s genetic diversity, or authorize it to protect established sailing and adaptive-paddling recreation?

A regional government must decide whether to cancel a planned causeway-and-bridge link between a populated island and the mainland. Most of the crossing would be solid embankment, leaving only a short bridge over the navigation channel. If built, the embankments would close most of the shallow sound's tidal cross-section. Flow would scour eelgrass near the bridge, while reduced circulation would deposit sediment behind the causeways and narrow tidal channels. The continuous shallow-water route linking the outer bay, eelgrass beds, and tidal-creek nurseries would be broken, disrupting juvenile fish movement and invertebrate dispersal.

Cancelling the project would preserve tidal exchange and connected habitat. Islanders would retain safe, subsidized, year-round passenger and vehicle ferries, but would continue to face fares, queues, busy-period bookings, sailing intervals, limited vehicle space, an overnight gap, and occasional weather reductions. Building the link would allow direct road, bus, bicycle, and pedestrian travel at any hour. Several culverts would still concentrate flow and leave depositional zones. A fully elevated bridge needs long grades for navigation clearance, but the island approach reaches the existing village before the bridge could return to ground level; a lower bridge would obstruct navigation. Closely spaced foundations in deep soft sediment would also disturb eelgrass and redirect shallow flow. Ferry subsidies cannot provide spontaneous overnight vehicle travel.

Should the regional government cancel the fixed link to protect habitat connectivity, or build it to protect islanders' mobility?

A remote Indigenous coastal community operates salmon pens in a shallow lagoon under its marine tenure. Eelgrass around the pens supports an amphipod found nowhere else. When recurring sea-lice outbreaks exceed mandatory fish-health thresholds, the elected Indigenous governing council must decide whether to permit a crustacean-targeting bath pesticide. Tarpaulins contain treatment during dosing, but the spent water must then be released. In the weakly flushed lagoon, it reaches every occupied eelgrass bed and kills amphipods faster than they reproduce. Repeated treatments would drive the species to extinction.

If the council denies permits, affected pens must be harvested early, emptied, and fallowed. Lower harvest weights and idle periods reduce production, interrupt processing, and cause rotating layoffs, fewer shifts, and lost vessel and maintenance contracts. Income guarantees and housing and utility protections prevent severe deprivation, but do not restore dependable work or commerce. Timing treatment outside breeding periods does not solve the problem because multiple amphipod life stages remain year-round and lice outbreaks are not seasonal. Treating fewer pens still contaminates every bed, onboard filtration has not reached a safe concentration, the nearest licensed receiving facility is beyond the vessels' range, and the council's tenure and certified moorings do not permit moving the pens offshore.

Should the council deny pesticide permits to protect the endemic species, or authorize discharge to protect local economic stability?

Several upland villages maintain a centuries-old spring sheep drive from valley farms to common summer grazing grounds. Families walk the inherited multi-day route together, observing rituals at stopping places, sharing meals, and teaching route-specific herding knowledge to younger participants. The route has twelve unavoidable stream and ford crossings within a headwater protection district. Steep slopes, unstable banks, and the absence of alternative passage rights prevent rerouting, and temporary bridges cannot span most of the crossings. Because tick pressure is high, veterinary movement rules allow the prolonged, close-contact drive only when flocks receive an effective full-duration treatment. The only locally registered treatment that works for the full journey is a persistent synthetic-pyrethroid dip applied at licensed facilities in the district.

If a regional planning commission issues seasonal permits for the dip, residues from treated fleece will enter the low-flow streams through rain and repeated crossings; keeping treated sheep entirely out of the water is infeasible. Sensitive aquatic arthropods will suffer major losses, reducing leaf-litter processing and aquatic prey production. Trout recruitment will weaken, while dippers and insectivorous bats will lose productive feeding areas, diminishing the connected headwater food web.

If the commission denies the permits, flocks may be transported by truck to enclosed summer grazing, retaining flock ownership and grazing access. But the walked drive, its stopping-place rituals, and its intergenerational teaching will cease. Should the regional planning commission deny the permits to protect headwater trophic integrity, or issue them to protect the villages’ cultural practice?

Cedar Ravine contains a temperate rainforest of centuries-old trees, layered canopy, nurse logs, specialist lichens, and moisture-dependent forest-floor communities. Although its canopy survives, the municipal downhill-cycling park has compacted trail corridors, drainage cuts, bridges, berms, and cleared sightlines that divide the understory and alter water movement. If the municipal council permanently closes the park and restores the area, it can remove the trail structures, regrade drainage cuts, loosen compacted soil carefully, replace woody debris, and replant native understory. These measures would reconnect forest-floor habitat, disperse runoff, reduce erosion and drying around old-tree roots, and restore the moist, shaded conditions on which the ravine’s old-growth assemblage depends. They would protect an irreplaceable long-established ecosystem, though they cannot recreate its ancient trees.

Closing the park would also remove the only nearby advanced downhill network used several times each week by local riders and a youth club for technical riding, exercise, instruction, competitions, and social gatherings. Gentler municipal paths remain available, and some riders could travel more than an hour to comparable facilities, but those alternatives cannot sustain the club’s regular advanced training and events. Retaining the complete system would preserve this affordable local recreational community, but continued riding and maintenance would keep the corridors compacted and drainage concentrated, progressively weakening the ravine’s humid, connected forest-floor processes.

A municipal survey found that any continuous advanced descent would cross saturated old-tree root zones, so retaining even one route would preserve a principal compacted corridor and leave restored areas hydrologically divided. Should the municipal council choose restoration that protects the old-growth ecosystem or continued operation that protects local downhill recreation?

A river-basin authority must decide whether to cancel a planned secondary embankment along a broad Central European river. The embankment would keep ordinary overbank floods from reaching twenty-nine privately owned hay parcels, equipment sheds, and two seasonal farm shops. Without it, shallow, forecastable floods will continue to disrupt harvests, require equipment to be moved and buildings cleaned, temporarily block customer access, and reduce rental and resale values. The properties are not primary residences and remain usable, but their established agricultural and commercial uses will remain materially unreliable.

Cancelling the project would leave the active floodplain connected to moderate floods. Those floods deposit and expose fresh, moist sediment where seeds from numerous European black poplar trees can establish. This process sustains the basin’s last large naturally reproducing stand, preserving rare genotypes and creating new genetic combinations as older trees die. If the embankment is built, the recruitment area will no longer receive the sediment-bearing floods that create these seedbeds. Sexual recruitment will largely cease, and replacement will depend mainly on vegetative shoots from a limited number of surviving genotypes, progressively reducing this population’s documented genetic breadth.

Should the river-basin authority cancel the embankment to protect the black poplar population’s genetic diversity, or construct it to protect the owners’ reliable use and value of their property?

On a small inhabited limestone island, the national government must decide the future of the only undeveloped parcel adjoining the cargo wharf. The parcel contains the island’s largest contiguous native coastal limestone scrub community, where salt-tolerant shrubs, endemic herbs, ground orchids, and seasonal annuals grow across shallow calcareous soils from the exposed shore to sheltered inland pockets. Designating it a permanent no-build reserve would preserve its characteristic species composition, seed banks, runoff patterns, and coastal-to-inland zonation.

The alternative is to authorize a refrigerated food depot with cold-storage rooms, a loading apron, fire access, drainage, utilities, and secure road access. Construction would remove most of the scrub through soil stripping and bedrock grading; altered drainage, vehicle disturbance, and weeds would leave disconnected margins dominated by disturbance-tolerant plants. Yet the depot would allow imported vegetables, fruit, dairy products, and other perishables to move directly into powered cooling. Reduced heat exposure and handling would lower prices and make these foods more consistently available to low-income residents, who currently face recurrent multiday stock gaps, higher costs, less varied shelf-stable diets, and extra shopping trips.

Should the national government designate the parcel as a permanent ecological reserve or authorize the depot to improve reliable, affordable access to perishable food?

A remote Indigenous community’s elected governing council must decide how to manage beavers in a boreal peatland surrounding an inherited cluster of twelve permanent homes on a low gravel ridge. Three beaver dam complexes have raised water across shallow peat divides, joining formerly intermittent ponds into a perennial wetland corridor. As long as the colonies and dams persist, the corridor retains connected sedge and willow habitat, movement routes for amphibians and aquatic invertebrates, waterfowl use, nutrient exchange, and pathways for recolonization among ponds. Yet the same impoundments keep groundwater above the surveyed limits for the homes’ foundations and wastewater fields.

The council can prohibit all community harvesting of beavers in the three-dam complex and relocate the households to completed higher-ground homes near the main village, with moving assistance and compensation. No one would be left homeless or in unsafe housing, but the move would permanently end residence in the established ridge cluster beside relatives, the meeting house, and family places. Alternatively, the council can authorize a recurring managed harvest and dam breaching sufficient to keep the homes within habitation standards. The households could remain safely in their current community, but the dams would no longer maintain the impoundments: peat between the ponds would dry seasonally, and the wetland corridor would become separate basins with reduced exchange of water, organisms, and ecological processes.

Should the elected Indigenous governing council choose the harvest ban that protects wetland continuity or the managed harvest that protects the households’ continued residence?

A regional government must decide the future of an obsolete irrigation dam above a Mediterranean delta. Although a newer off-channel system supplies downstream irrigation, the old reservoir traps nearly all coarse sand and gravel from the catchment. Removing the dam through staged drawdown would release suitable stored sediment gradually and allow future bedload to reach the coast. Waves and currents would again distribute material across the delta front, lagoon entrances, and shallow seabeds, reducing the sediment deficit, supporting shallow sand habitat and lagoon margins, and slowing erosion and fragmentation along exposed seagrass edges. The restored process would strengthen the connected marine habitat mosaic used by seagrass-edge communities, infauna, nursery fish, lagoon organisms, and their predators.

Retaining the dam would keep the reservoir at its stable managed level. That would preserve the lake-based economy of a nearby delta town: campsites, rowing clubs, cafés, equipment rentals, and seasonal events, along with the maintenance contractors, suppliers, retailers, and employees they support. Removal would replace the lake with a narrower, seasonally variable river corridor; the existing rowing courses, campsites, launching areas, and event venues could no longer operate in their current locations. Visitor spending would decline, some small firms would close or become seasonal, and workers and owners would face job changes and less predictable incomes.

Should the regional government remove the dam to protect the marine ecosystem or retain it to protect local economic stability?

Four municipalities share the Orenda estuary, whose narrow central reach contains the entire known range of the Orenda burrowing goby. This endemic fish breeds by excavating burrows in exposed, soft vertical banks. High-speed passenger ferries use the narrows on the fastest public-transport route from residential towns to the main employment and rail center. Their wakes undercut and slump the banks faster than natural deposition can rebuild them, destroying nests during breeding and leaving too little intact habitat for the following season. Continued high-speed operation reduces occupied habitat below the level associated with stable recruitment.

The intermunicipal public authority can designate the narrows as an aquatic protected area and require ferries to travel at displacement speed year-round. That rule would keep wakes below the bank-failure threshold, allowing breeding burrows, eggs, and juvenile shelter to persist across the goby’s only occupied reach. Ferry travel would continue, but approximately 3,100 regular passengers would face crossings about 22 minutes longer, less practical rail transfers, and less frequent evening service. They use the route for work, education, appointments, and family travel; an indirect road route remains available. Alternatively, the authority can leave the corridor outside the protected area, retaining fast crossings, existing evening frequency, and coordinated rail connections while the goby’s breeding habitat continues to decline.

Should the intermunicipal public authority designate the protected area and impose the speed rule, or continue high-speed ferry service to protect passengers’ mobility?

A county seeks permits for a permanent haul road across a spring-fed limestone basin connecting public roads to privately managed woodland. The basin contains an intact native calcareous-fen community of sedges, orchids, low shrubs, and marl-pool plants. Its continuous vegetation mosaic depends on low-nutrient groundwater spreading diffusely through shallow peat and marl. A raised, compacted road embankment would interrupt that flow, while cross-drains would concentrate it at isolated points. Part of the fen would become drier and another part more persistently flooded and nutrient-enriched; reeds and woody vegetation would expand as specialized fen plants decline, converting much of the basin into reedbed, scrub, and simplified wetland patches.

Several logging crews and family woodland operators depend on the woodland beyond the basin for a substantial recurring share of their income. They need dependable access for harvesting equipment, timber trucks, and rescue vehicles to maintain selective-harvest rotations and regular crew employment. Without the road, steep and rocky approaches cannot safely accommodate those vehicles, and the stands would no longer be commercially harvestable. Contracts, crew hours, and family woodland income would decline durably, though the affected people would retain their homes and some work or income elsewhere.

The environmental regulatory agency must decide whether to deny the indispensable permits, cancelling the road and preserving the native fen community, or approve them and protect the operators’ established livelihoods: should it choose the ecologically protective option or the option protecting the human interest?

An Indigenous community’s ancestral coastal cemetery occupies the last intact stabilized dune in its territory. Its remaining unoccupied burial plots overlap the only wild population of a genetically distinct lineage of a regionally widespread dune violet. Flowering plants and a persistent seed bank extend across nearly all stable ground suitable for additional graves. Each excavation, along with spoil placement and new access paths, would destroy rooted plants and buried seeds. As plots are used, the remaining patches would become too sparse and separated for reliable pollen exchange and recruitment, ultimately eliminating this distinct local lineage and its rare alleles.

Families have an established tradition of burying relatives beside ancestors in the coastal cemetery. An accessible inland community cemetery can accommodate future burials and allows funerals and local interment to continue, but it cannot provide continuity with the existing ancestral graves. Closing the coastal plots would permanently end this place-based form of ancestral burial for future relatives. Continuing approvals until the plots are occupied would allow the practice to continue for those families receiving them, while destroying most of the violet lineage’s sole habitat.

The elected Indigenous governing council administers both cemeteries and can either close the remaining coastal plots, protect the dune, and direct future burials inland, or continue approving coastal burials. Should the council choose the ecologically protective closure or the option that protects families’ ancestral burial practice?

On a humid volcanic island, the only high-voltage line from a geothermal plant to six eastern villages crosses roadless cloud-forest gullies. Three headwater streams beneath the corridor contain the entire known population of an endemic stream salamander. Under the current pesticide license, persistent broadleaf herbicide is applied to maintain conductor clearances. Wet-season storms carry residues and contaminated sediment into the streams at concentrations that kill salamander larvae and their aquatic invertebrate prey. Recruitment fails in the two most affected streams, leaving a single small, isolated population vulnerable to drought, disease, and storms.

The regional government can instead prohibit the herbicide and require rope-access manual cutting during planned de-energization periods. This would allow breeding to continue in all three streams and preserve connectivity across the salamander’s complete known range. Yet manual cutting would triple vegetation-management costs and require about eighteen planned four-hour daytime shutdowns each wet season. Higher regulated tariffs and repeated interruptions would disrupt refrigeration, home working, retail activity, and small electric machinery for households, shops, and workshops, though protected essential loads would remain supplied. Continuing the existing applications would retain current tariffs and continuous daytime power while preserving required conductor clearances.

Should the regional government choose the herbicide prohibition that protects the endemic salamander or continued applications that protect reliable, affordable energy access?

Across a river basin’s glacial plain, a twelve-kilometre chain of seasonal prairie potholes is connected by shallow grassed swales running through seven family-owned grain farms. A river-basin authority can designate the potholes, swales, and necessary hydrological buffers as a protected wetland complex. If it does, spring sheet flows and varied wetland conditions will persist across the chain, sustaining shallow-water, mudflat, grass, and sedge habitats. Aquatic invertebrates, amphibians, and breeding waterbirds will continue to use the wetlands as a connected system, including for movement and recolonization after drought years.

Designation would also permanently prohibit drainage and cultivation within the mapped areas. The families would retain their homes, ownership, and viable farm operations, but protected strips and wet pockets would reduce workable acreage and machinery efficiency. Their recurring income, resale value, borrowing value, and freedom to decide future uses of portions of their land would decline.

If the authority declines designation, the owners may install tile systems permitted under ordinary agricultural rules and cultivate the swales. They could drain persistently waterlogged ground, consolidate fields, improve machinery use, stabilize yields, and preserve the ordinary productive and financial value of their property. Yet tile drainage would eliminate several intermediate potholes, shorten inundation in others, and leave surviving basins hydrologically isolated, with simplified seasonal habitats and fewer opportunities for amphibians and aquatic invertebrates to move across the chain. Should the river-basin authority designate the protected wetland complex or decline designation to protect the families’ property interests?

Five coastal towns share an Atlantic inlet where mature blue-mussel reefs provide the principal persistent hard substrate amid mobile sand and mud. The reefs are built from living mussels, bound shell, and accumulated shell layers. Their recovery would restore substantial vertical and spatial complexity, supporting attached algae, worms, small crustaceans, juvenile fish, and feeding birds, while strengthening filtration, biodeposition, nutrient exchange, and resistance to winter disturbance. Monitoring shows that six consecutive years without removal of large mussels would allow surviving beds to form the bound shell layers needed for this recovery.

Twenty-four licensed hand gatherers from long-established fishing families depend on wild mussels for a substantial share of household income. The lowest annual catch that covers operating and purification costs and maintains regular restaurant and wholesale orders would keep their occupation viable, preserving their skills, licenses, arrangements, and buyers. Yet that catch would continue removing large mussels and new structure faster than multilayered reefs can form, leaving shallow, patchy beds vulnerable to winter burial and dislodgment. A six-year inlet-wide ban would end all legal wild catch; closure payments and seasonal work would meet basic needs but would not preserve full income, active commercial gathering, or established customer relationships.

Should the intermunicipal public authority impose the six-year harvest ban to protect the marine ecosystem, or continue the commercially viable harvest to protect the gatherers’ livelihood?

In an inland arid basin, groundwater-fed alkali meadows beside a small town contain a characteristic mosaic of saltgrass, sedges, rushes, and native forbs. Their wet-to-dry zonation depends on groundwater remaining above several spring outlets. Current permitted pumping for local irrigation keeps groundwater near or below those elevations. If an environmental regulatory agency renews present allocations without reserving water for the springs, most meadow surfaces will lose spring-fed moisture. Sedges and moisture-dependent forbs will progressively disappear as salt accumulation expands bare patches and shrubs and disturbance-tolerant weeds replace much of the meadow mosaic.

The same aquifer supports dairies and feed-growing operations, along with repair shops, suppliers, and haulers. These lawful businesses depend on predictable irrigation production, and their workers and owners have organized employment, contracts, loans, and income around longstanding permits. The agency can instead impose a basin-wide pumping limit for at least ten years, reserving enough groundwater to sustain spring discharge and the meadow community. That decision would reduce irrigation allocations, contract fodder production and herd capacity, and is expected to lead one dairy and several feed-growing operations to close or cease local production. Recurring work and business income would decline for several years, although transition payments and support would prevent acute deprivation. Renewing current allocations would preserve established production, shifts, contracts, and local trade, while allowing the meadow springs to fail.

Should the environmental regulatory agency choose the ecological groundwater reserve that protects the native plant community or renew current allocations to protect local economic stability?

On a cool oceanic peninsula, two rows of 28 legally built, permanently occupied cottages stand on the only sand-covered saddle linking intact foredunes to inland dune slacks. The saddle once carried windblown sand between these areas. Its foundations, retaining walls, roads, buried utilities, gardens, and sand fencing now interrupt that movement. As a result, older slacks accumulate organic matter and scrub without being replaced by young slacks, leaving the peninsula-endemic sand earwig with a small peripheral population and a progressively reduced range of breeding and drought-refuge habitat.

A regional planning commission can either approve a funded managed-retreat and restoration plan or renew permanent residential status and utility protection for the block. Restoration would require acquiring all cottages at replacement value, providing moving expenses and comparable homes in nearby towns, and removing the structures and obstructions so the saddle can be regraded. Seasonal sand transport would then resume, producing shifting dry dunes, disturbed sand, and moist young slacks used by the earwig. Residents would retain access to employment and services but would lose their current homes, coastal setting, and compact mutual-aid community.

Renewing residential protection would allow every household to remain, preserving familiar surroundings and neighbor-support arrangements. Yet the stabilized saddle would remain, and the principal habitat-forming process for the endemic species would stay disabled. Should the regional planning commission choose habitat restoration for the sand earwig or protect the residents’ ability to remain in their homes?

A remote river city's municipal council must decide the future of the lowest lock-and-dam on its freight canal. The structure creates the navigation pool that lets shallow-draft barges deliver flour, rice, pulses, and cooking oil directly to the central food terminal. Removing it would force smaller truck shipments from a distant railhead over a long mountain route, raising prices and causing recurring stock gaps. Residents would still have enough food, but staples would be less affordable and accessible, especially for low-income households and people unable to reach distant supermarkets.

The dam divides a native sturgeon population into two small breeding groups that retain different uncommon alleles. The operating lock provides no reliable upstream passage and little downstream juvenile passage. Removal would restore recurring movement and interbreeding; retention would allow genetic drift to narrow the population's inherited traits. Scheduled lock openings do not work: telemetry shows that adults do not reliably enter the lock, while juveniles disperse when its gates remain closed. The only low-gradient bypass corridor is occupied by the terminal apron and floodwall, whose removal would itself end barge unloading. A new railhead terminal is also unavailable because its direct approach crosses a weight-restricted historic bridge, while the adequate route requires the same long mountain detour.

Should the council remove the lock-and-dam to protect sturgeon genetic diversity, or retain it to protect reliable, affordable access to staple foods?

A state or provincial natural-resources agency must decide whether to cancel a planned tidal-energy barrage across the narrow mouth of a northern macrotidal bay. The barrage would restrict the volume and timing of tidal exchange, reducing tidal range and current velocities. Feeding flats would no longer drain normally, fine sediment would accumulate over suspension-feeding beds, bottom-water flushing would weaken, and movement between the bay and open sea would be obstructed. Benthic prey, migratory fish, and diving birds would decline across a marine ecosystem whose flats, channels, marshes, and food web depend on natural tidal processes.

Cancelling the project would preserve the bay’s tidal range, reversing currents, salinity exchange, sediment transport, oxygen renewal, and seasonal movement of marine organisms. Yet six coastal towns would remain dependent on an aging transmission line, imported power, and costly oil-fired generators during winter peaks. Essential electricity and heating would continue through protected circuits and backup supply, but households and businesses would face higher bills, recurring conservation periods, scheduled curtailments of nonessential loads, and reduced operating hours for some energy-intensive businesses.

If the agency proceeds, predictable tidal generation would cover the towns’ modeled winter shortfall, reduce oil use, lessen curtailments, and support more affordable electricity, heating, and commercial activity. Hydrodynamic modeling indicates that openings large enough to preserve the tidal prism and peak currents needed for normal drainage, sediment transport, and flushing would leave too little hydraulic head and turbine throughput to cover that shortfall. Should the agency cancel the barrage to protect the marine ecosystem or build it to protect energy access for the coastal towns?

A municipal council must decide whether to ban the uprooting, cutting, and collection of native marram throughout a migrating dune neck that contains the only direct road between an outer residential district and the town center. If it adopts the ban and retires the road, windblown sand will bury the unused carriageway and marram will spread across it. This will create continuous vegetated dune substrate between northern and southern habitats, allowing flightless sand-running beetles, dune spiders, and other ground-dwelling dune specialists to disperse without crossing an exposed road corridor.

If the council instead permits recurring removal of marram and rhizomes from the road margins, along with routine sand clearance, the direct road and municipal bus will remain open. Residents, care workers, tradespeople, students, and bus passengers will retain current journey times, fares, service frequency, and convenient access to work, education, care, shops, and municipal services. Maintaining the road, however, will preserve a broad, compacted or paved strip with bare safety margins, where heat, unsuitable substrate, lack of shelter, and traffic keep the two dune habitats functionally disconnected. Under the ban, travelers would remain connected to necessities and emergency services through an inland loop, but each trip would take about 30–45 minutes longer, with higher travel costs, reduced bus convenience, and a longer, more weather-exposed walking and cycling route.

Should the municipal council choose the harvest ban and road retirement to restore habitat connectivity, or continued marram removal to protect everyday mobility?

A public desert plateau contains a long-continuous mosaic of centuries-old cushion shrubs, mature hummock grasses, biological soil crusts, undisturbed soil horizons, and connected burrow networks. Its natural runoff patterns support these slowly formed structures, which cannot be recreated on commercial or community-planning time scales. A narrow seam of dimension stone lies beneath the central intact tract. If the public land-management authority withdraws the tract from leasing and prohibits quarry roads, excavation, blasting, spoil placement, and heavy-vehicle use, the old-growth ecosystem and its slow ecological dynamics will remain intact.

The nearby quarry town’s current stone source is nearly exhausted. Its processing sheds require the nearby seam’s particular block size, strength, fracture pattern, and appearance; comparable stone from elsewhere would cost more than the local businesses can absorb. Without a new lease, skilled quarry and cutting jobs will fall sharply, freight and repair demand will contract, and linked shops and service firms will face sustained closures, lower incomes, and unstable municipal revenue. Temporary support can prevent acute deprivation but cannot preserve the town’s production relationships and commercial activity.

Alternatively, the authority can issue a fifteen-year lease and authorize the pit, overburden removal, spoil terraces, haul road, and operating area. This would sustain the town’s principal skilled industry and linked businesses, but excavation would remove the ecosystem within its footprint and fragment adjoining areas through altered runoff, dust, vibration, and traffic. Should the public land-management authority protect the old-growth plateau or protect the town’s local economic stability?

A state natural-resources agency must decide whether to designate a sheltered island reef complex as a permanent no-take marine protected area. The reef is the region’s principal juvenile habitat for large wrasses and spiny lobsters and includes the deeper reef where adults forage. These predators keep grazing urchins below the density at which kelp recruitment fails. If the agency closes the connected nursery and foraging grounds to commercial take, wrasses and lobsters will recover above that threshold. Kelp beds will persist, sustaining habitat and feeding relationships among producers, invertebrates, reef fishes, and seabirds.

If the agency declines designation, regulated trapping and hook fishing will continue under existing rules. Continued removal will keep predator numbers below the control threshold, allowing urchins to consume new kelp and leaving extensive barrens and a simplified food web. Yet the closure would also remove the only nearby reef that twenty-eight licensed owner-operated boats can reliably work during winter, when offshore grounds are unsafe. Several owners would leave commercial fishing, deckhand jobs would disappear, and the dockside live-seafood buyer would close or operate only seasonally. Transition grants would protect basic needs but would not preserve these fishing occupations or businesses.

Four municipalities jointly manage a sheltered cove where historic dredging and removed moorings left a broad scar of bare seabed between surviving inner and outer eelgrass beds. The intermunicipal public authority can restore the scarred band by seeding and transplanting native eelgrass, using temporary anchoring grids while it establishes, and permanently prohibiting hauled seines across the restored corridor. The plants would reconnect the beds into a continuous belt of protective feeding structure, allowing juvenile fish, pipefish, small crustaceans, and eelgrass-associated epifauna to move, disperse, and recolonize across the cove under cover rather than crossing exposed sediment.

The same shallow arc and gently shelving beach are the setting for the four towns’ annual communal beach-seine harvest and shore feast. Fishing families, hauling crews, cooks, craftspeople, and residents prepare the net, haul it together, teach younger participants, divide the lawful catch ceremonially, and share the feast. The weighted footrope must sweep the central band to keep fish from escaping; it would uproot eelgrass shoots, cut rhizomes, and reopen the gap. A narrow lane, altered footrope, reseeding after the event, or another shore would not preserve the established practice or the restored corridor. If the authority leaves the sweep bare and renews the permit, the annual haul continues in its customary form, but habitat connectivity remains reduced.

A humid mountain plateau’s privately held tea estates lie on steep slopes above a basin of old-growth cloud forest. The forest’s massive uneven-aged trees, acidic organic mats, epiphyte communities, fungi, microfauna, and slow nutrient processes reflect centuries of continuity and cannot be recreated quickly. Persistent copper fungicide applied on the tea fields is carried by heavy rainfall in fine particles and colloids into the basin. The forest’s organic mats retain it, and repeated inputs simplify sensitive fungal and microfaunal communities, slow litter processing, and weaken the regeneration and substrate-forming processes that sustain the old-growth ecosystem.

A regional planning commission can prohibit this fungicide throughout the mapped recharge and runoff area. Doing so would sharply reduce new copper loading and permit a gradual decline in bioavailable copper, supporting eventual recovery of sensitive soil communities and the forest processes they sustain. Yet the wettest contiguous tea blocks depend on the treatment: available substitute fungicides wash off in persistent rain, and untreated disease makes their tea commercially unreliable. Owners and lawful operators would lose recurring production, processing sheds would operate below established throughput, lease income would decline where applicable, and the properties’ dependable agricultural and collateral value would fall, though substantial drier fields, buildings, access, and basic economic security would remain.

Should the regional planning commission prohibit the persistent copper fungicide to protect the old-growth cloud forest, or allow its continued label-compliant use to protect the tea estates’ productive property value?

After household water, sanitation, and dam-safety requirements are met, an elected Indigenous governing council must allocate a fixed dry-season volume from a dam above its coastal settlement. It can spread that water as a continuous low release for five years, maintaining freshwater input to the narrow marine estuary between tides. This would preserve the salinity gradient, limit low-oxygen stratification, keep eelgrass-edge sediments oxygenated, and sustain shellfish filtration, burrowing invertebrates, amphipods, and feeding and refuge habitat for juvenile coastal fish. The flow would be too shallow, however, to cover fixed boulder hazards in the gorge.

Alternatively, the council can retain the established twice-monthly weekend pulses that make local whitewater descents safe. These releases allow volunteer instruction and an affordable, intergenerational recreational practice to continue without ferry travel and overnight accommodation on another island. Yet the long intervals with negligible inflow would leave saline bottom water stratified over organic sediments, depleting oxygen and creating sulfide-rich conditions. Much of the burrowing fauna would be eliminated, eelgrass margins would thin, shellfish function and amphipod production would decline, and the estuary would become a substantially simplified marine community. Brief pulses cannot prevent this damage. Intermediate schedules cannot provide both safe paddling flows and the continuous estuarine threshold.

Should the elected Indigenous governing council choose the continuous release that protects the marine ecosystem or the twice-monthly pulses that protect local recreation?

A state-managed miombo woodland reserve surrounds four rural villages where edible caterpillars emerge densely on mature host trees during each rainy season. Families currently collect and dry them as their cheapest locally available animal protein, relying on stored supplies when roads and market deliveries are unreliable. For low-income households without regular vehicle access, ending collection would mean greater dependence on beans, eggs, dried fish, and similar foods from irregular mobile vendors, raising expenses and creating recurring gaps in affordable protein. Staples and relief foods would still prevent starvation or medically dangerous deprivation.

The public land-management authority can either continue the authorized household harvest or impose a six-year, reserve-wide collection ban. Continued harvesting removes most late-instar caterpillars before peak predation, parasitoid emergence, and frass deposition. Bird, lizard, and small-mammal breeding and recruitment decline; parasitoids become too sparse to maintain their role; and decomposer activity weakens beneath host trees, simplifying the connected canopy-to-soil food web. A ban would leave most caterpillars for predators and parasitoids and maintain frass and remains for decomposers, allowing these trophic relationships to recover and function through variable emergence years. Limited allowances cannot meet both needs, and quotas or spatial rotation cannot be effectively enforced or sustain the required ecological pathways.

Should the public land-management authority impose the harvest ban to protect trophic integrity, or continue household harvesting to protect villagers’ food access?

On a cool, treeless island, a nearly continuous blanket bog runs from upland seepages to coastal flushes. Its remaining uncut peat ridges and adjoining recharge areas hold saturated peat at the elevation needed to pass water between bog basins. If these areas are permanently closed to extraction, peat-forming vegetation, linked wet margins, and connected habitat for wetland invertebrates and birds will persist. Older peripheral cuttings can stabilize without new drainage faces advancing into the last hydrological links.

The island environmental regulatory agency can instead renew regulated household peat-cutting licences on those ridges for twenty years. They are the only accessible common plots still containing usable domestic fuel peat; older areas are exhausted, fragmented, or unreachable without new roads. Licensing would let low- and middle-income households continue using low-cost local fuel in existing stoves, comfortably heating their occupied rooms without relying as heavily on weather-delayed imports or costly building conversions. Yet successive cutting, grips, and drainage channels would breach the ridges, lower adjoining water tables, and divide the continuous bog into smaller wet remnants separated by heath, gullies, and bare peat.

A prohibition would end household peat cutting on the island. Imported briquettes or heating oil, a targeted allowance, and an emergency reserve would maintain safe temperatures, but households would spend about 12 percent more of their disposable income on heating, heat fewer rooms in winter, and lose a customary means of providing for themselves. Should the environmental regulatory agency choose permanent protection of the wetland links or renewed licences protecting households’ access to affordable local heating fuel?

A municipal council must decide the future of a century-old retired hydropower dam in an interior Pacific Northwest valley. The dam maintains a six-kilometre reservoir, but it also attenuates spring floods and traps gravel and large wood upstream. Downstream, an old-growth black cottonwood–western redcedar floodplain depends on seasonal flooding, mobile sediment, large wood, and shifting side channels. Continued impoundment means cottonwood recruitment and side-channel renewal will keep failing; as veteran trees die, the floodplain will lose its uneven-age structure, wet microsites, and disturbance processes. Complete removal of the dam, its sediment-retaining works, flow-control structures, and powerhouse foundation would restore the flood conditions and material movement that sustain this old-growth ecosystem.

Participants travel together from a waterfront longhouse to a burial bluff, teaching canoe handling, songs, protocols, and responsibilities during the calm-water journey and making a collective landing at the bluff. Removal would expose a shallow, boulder-strewn river with two rapids, permanently ending the unified flotilla, ceremonial approach, landing, and route-specific teaching, though both sites would remain accessible by land. Retaining the dam would preserve the gathering in its established form but allow the old-growth floodplain to continue declining.

In a monsoon river basin, flooded terraced rice fields and gravity-fed ditches form the only wet-season shallow-water connection between two natural marshes. Native climbing perch use this chain of paddies as habitat for movement, breeding exchange, and recolonization after drying. If the river-basin authority prohibits aquatic molluscicide throughout the corridor, the fish can cross the full chain during the monsoon. Wet-season irrigation and flooding will continue under existing tenancy agreements even if rice production declines.

Apple snails, however, consume newly transplanted rice. Without molluscicide, repeated replanting, lower yields, and unreliable receipts will deprive tenant households of a substantial share of their established farm income. Transplanting and harvesting crews will receive far fewer paid days, and the village mill will operate below the level needed for regular staffing. Housing, food support, and transition assistance will prevent severe deprivation, but rice farming and milling will no longer continue at their established occupational scale. Local trials found that untreated stepping-stone paddies allowed snails to recolonize neighboring fields before seedlings became resistant, while screens, hand collection, ducks, and older seedlings did not keep losses below the farms’ viability threshold. Permitting synchronized molluscicide application immediately after transplanting would sustain viable harvests, regular seasonal work, and the mill’s commercial throughput, but several consecutive paddies and connecting ditches would become acutely toxic during the principal fish-movement period, functionally disconnecting the two marsh populations across successive monsoons.

Should the river-basin authority prohibit molluscicide to protect habitat connectivity or permit it to protect established livelihoods?

Seven municipalities share a mountain reservoir whose spring allocation determines flows through a broad downstream floodplain. The only low terrace across which water can reach the floodplain’s principal side channels and ponds is occupied by a lawful 34-home riverside hamlet. Its residents include multigenerational households whose gardens, workshop spaces, community hall, and daily networks of informal care are concentrated there.

An intermunicipal public authority can allocate stored water to a six-week annual overbank pulse. The resulting inundation would reconnect the river, side channels, and floodplain ponds, allowing cottonwood and willow recruitment, aquatic-insect production, amphibian breeding, juvenile-fish feeding, and the seasonal transfer of prey to herons, otters, and terrestrial predators. This would maintain a functioning food web across channel and floodplain habitats. But the same releases would inundate yards, the sole access road, wellheads, and septic fields, so the authority would have to acquire the properties and relocate residents beforehand. Replacement-value compensation, suitable homes, and moving support would prevent homelessness, yet the residents would lose their established homes and compact community.

Alternatively, the authority can retain the spring volume for municipal supply and keep releases within the channel. Residents could remain, but the ponds would stay disconnected and stagnate or dry prematurely; food-web functions would substantially decline. Should the intermunicipal public authority choose the overbank release that protects trophic integrity or the within-channel allocation that protects residents’ continued residence?

On a windswept northern archipelago, a national government must decide the future of a state-owned lodgepole-pine fuelwood estate covering the headwaters and central drainage corridor of a lowland watershed. Ending fuelwood rotations would allow the government to remove pine, block plantation drains, selectively remove needle-rich litter where needed, and reseed local heath species. A connected mosaic of dry and wet native heath would return across the watershed, replacing the uniform exotic conifer crop with characteristic plant communities and restored moisture gradients. If harvesting and drainage continue, canopy shade, acidic needles, and pine seed rain will keep the watershed dominated by plantation vegetation, while only small heath remnants remain at its edges.

The estate provides the nonreplaceable majority of the wood chips used by the cooperative district-heating plant serving the main settlement. Continuing rotations would preserve a dependable local fuel supply, stable tariffs, and winter chip reserves for households, a school, food stores, and small workshops. Restoration would require imported compressed biomass and electric backup after temporary clearance material is used, causing persistent tariff increases, smaller winter reserves, and reduced heating of secondary spaces during expensive weeks. Subsidies, tariff support, and minimum-service guarantees would prevent disconnection and dangerous indoor cold, but lower-income residents in old stone buildings and local enterprises would still bear substantial costs. Should the national government choose watershed-scale restoration of the native heath community or continued fuelwood production to protect affordable, reliable heat?

On three neighboring islands in a subtropical volcanic archipelago, an endemic grazing topshell lives only on wave-cut basalt benches. Adolescents from coastal clans traditionally gather live shells at named family shores for their coming-of-age ceremonies. With elder shell workers, they drill and polish the shells into ceremonial belts, then wear the belts in a public presentation. The practice joins a personal journey, family place, skilled work, oral instruction, and recognition as an adult.

The regional planning commission can either retain cultural permits or impose a twelve-year ban on taking live topshells throughout the shoreline management zones. Permitted collection must use large adults, since smaller shells split during drilling and the established belt already uses the minimum number required. Yet these large shells are the most fecund breeders. Continued annual collection keeps adult density below the fertilization threshold on two islands, suppressing recruitment and larval contribution and leaving the species concentrated on the third island. A ban would allow breeding adults on the depleted islands to recover, restoring recruitment and strengthening the connected population.

Under a ban, ceremonies could continue with inherited belts, replicas, or imported shells, but initiates could not gather and make their own belts from family shores, interrupting the locally specific practice for more than a decade. Several established settlements on stable islands along a subarctic river delta are planned to receive a twelve-kilometer all-season gravel road to the regional highway. The approved design requires a raised embankment above spring flood levels, with bridges at major distributaries and culverts across sedge marshes, thaw ponds, minor channels, and areas of diffuse sheet flow. Water would remain longer upstream, while downstream marshes and ponds would receive less water and sediment; faster culvert flows would replace many shallow connections. The roadbed would also persistently divide wetland units, simplifying vegetation patterns and reducing connectivity among aquatic and semi-aquatic populations.

If the regional government cancels the road before tendering, spring floods would continue to spread through the connected mosaic of channels, ponds, and marshes, allowing water, sediment, fish, invertebrates, and semi-aquatic animals to move across the delta margin. Building the road would instead provide year-round vehicle travel for work, appointments, shopping, and family responsibilities.

A state natural-resources agency must decide whether to designate a lagoon’s central oyster shoal and its reef links as a no-dredge aquatic protected area. The lagoon’s native oyster species would persist with its distinct salinity-associated lineages and a broader range of genetic combinations.

The designation would also prevent the harbor from deepening a channel needed by replacement freight vessels. No other navigable alignment can meet the required width, curvature, and depth without crossing the shoal. Should the state natural-resources agency choose the protected area that preserves genetic diversity or approve the channel project that protects local economic stability?

Snowmobile clubs maintain warming huts along the routes. Nearby alternatives are fragmented or run along steep commercial-forest roads that many older riders, novice riders, and families cannot use safely or comfortably.

Elk then remain longer in the low-snow floodplain, browse willow beyond the threshold for its recruitment, and reduce the food and building material available to beavers. If the council reduces commercial pumping during the nine-month low-head visitor season to keep aquifer pressure above every vent, all three spring runs will remain wet. The amphipod will retain its full range, abundance, and genetically differentiated groups.

That allocation would leave most mineral-bath pools without sufficient mineral-water flow to meet mandatory turnover and cleaning requirements. Several of the five family concessions would close, while the rest could offer only limited sessions. A national government must decide whether to cancel an avalanche gallery and deflection berm planned above a historic twenty-seven-household hamlet. The only geotechnically viable alignment crosses a long-established subalpine larch-spruce forest. Building it would clear a broad corridor through centuries-old trees and snags, excavate old soils, remove nurse logs, sever fungal and root connections, and redirect smaller snow movements into damaging edge effects. The forest would remain, but its long-continuous structure and canopy mosaic would be permanently fragmented.

If the project is cancelled, hazard law requires the bench to become a no-residence zone. Households would receive completed serviced homes, acquisition payments, and moving help in the main village twelve kilometres away. They would avoid homelessness and avalanche exposure, but lose their homes, communal hall, workshops, neighboring family properties, and geographically dependent mutual-care arrangements. House reinforcement cannot withstand the design loads or keep the sole road and utilities operating. Warning or seasonal evacuation fails the residential standard because destructive releases can lack reliable lead time. A shorter berm directs snow toward eastern homes; moving it upslope reaches unstable bedrock and clears more old growth, while moving it downslope leaves homes in the runout. Compensation limits material loss but cannot preserve residence at the site.

Should the government cancel the project and relocate the hamlet to protect the old-growth forest, or build the defenses so residents can remain?

A municipal council must decide the future of an obsolete diversion dam across a perennial semiarid foothill arroyo. The dam’s concrete apron and walled banks divide the channel and interrupt the narrow cottonwood-willow corridor between perennial reaches. If the council removes the dam, apron, and walls and grades the municipal work area into a continuous low-flow channel and revegetated floodplain passage, native chub and mud turtles will be able to move between the upper and lower reaches during suitable flows. Riparian animals will also regain a sheltered route, allowing dispersal and recolonization after localized drought losses.

Four families own adjoining citrus and date orchards and lawfully pump irrigation water from shallow wells within the impoundment’s recharge footprint. Removing the dam would dissipate the groundwater mound that supports those wells, leaving them unable to provide irrigation volumes needed to maintain the mature trees economically. The families would retain their homes, land, and possible lower-value lawful uses, but would lose recurring harvest income, their investment in the mature orchards, and a substantial share of their parcels’ agricultural value. Repairing and retaining the dam at its existing pool elevation would preserve the wells, orchards, income, and ordinary agricultural use, but the barrier and break in riparian cover would remain.

Should the municipal council choose removal to protect habitat connectivity, or repair and retain the dam to protect the orchard owners’ property interest?

In a high-desert valley, a single spring supplies both a chain of sedge ciénegas and a four-century communal acequia used by three villages. During recurrent dry seasons, its discharge can either keep the wetlands’ connecting swales saturated or provide enough water for one viable cycle of heritage maize and chile cultivation, but not both. If a state or provincial natural-resources agency reserves the flow in the natural channel, shallow groundwater will continue connecting the ciénega cells. Sedge cover, aquatic-invertebrate exchange, amphibian movement, seed dispersal, and wetland soil processes will persist across the chain. If the agency instead diverts the water, the middle swales will dry each diversion season, progressively leaving isolated spring pools separated by eroding, shrub-filled dry gaps.

Delivering the allocation through the acequia would allow the villages to maintain their integrated annual practice: public assignment of irrigation turns, communal ditch maintenance, reciprocal field work, cultivation of their own heritage crops, and planting and harvest observances. Reserving water for the wetlands would leave too little for tail-end plots or a mature crop, interrupting that customary cycle, although households would remain in their homes, retain ordinary employment and food access, and receive compensation for crop losses. Dividing the flow or rotating it cannot meet either threshold.

Should the state or provincial natural-resources agency reserve the spring flow to protect wetland continuity or deliver it through the acequia to protect the villages’ cultural practice?

In a protected limestone mountain pass, a short public trail leads through a native meadow of cushion plants, bunchgrasses, orchids, gentians, and late-flowering asters. Local walking associations have long held midsummer hikes there, gathering small mixed bouquets for home display and an annual exhibition that tests field identification and arrangement skills. Participants follow existing permits and bouquet limits; the tradition is recreational, but it is a meaningful intergenerational social activity tied to this particular meadow.

Permit monitoring shows that collectors repeatedly select the largest, most conspicuous flowering stems before they set seed. Although long-lived adult forbs remain visible for a time, too few seedlings and younger plants replace them. As older plants die, bunchgrasses fill the gaps, progressively simplifying the meadow’s characteristic mixture of native forbs and grasses. A fifteen-year harvest ban would allow repeated flowering, seed production, and establishment, while leaving hiking, photography, and observation open. Yet it would make the associations’ gathering, specimen-based identification, and meadow-flower exhibition unlawful. Renewing the permits would preserve that accessible annual recreation but continue the pattern of inadequate recruitment. No intermediate harvest rule both sustains the defining activity and provides the consecutive undisturbed reproductive seasons the meadow requires.

Should an environmental regulatory agency impose the harvest ban to protect the native plant community, or renew the permits to protect the walking associations’ recreation?

On a nationally owned oceanic island, a degraded dry-forest plateau contains the principal surviving population of an endemic ebony. Its remaining groves hold distinct drought-, salt-, and disease-response variants, yet goats have consumed nearly all seedlings outside small fenced pockets for decades. Without restored connections between groves, old trees will die without replacement, rare variants will disappear, and the population will become smaller and genetically narrower.

Twenty-two licensed family businesses have grazed goats on the plateau for generations and comply with their stocking limits. Their herds support most of their income, as well as a small dairy, a hide workshop, and seasonal employment. If the national government renews the licences, the connected range, watering points, and access routes necessary for viable goat production will remain, preserving the businesses, their breeding stock, and their customer relationships. Landscape-scale dry-forest restoration will be forgone.

Alternatively, the government can decline renewal, remove the goats, stabilize eroded slopes, suppress invasive pasture plants, and restore native forest between the groves using seed from every grove. Ebony seedlings would survive, groves would regain sexually reproducing age classes, and their distinct variants would persist in a larger connected population. The families would receive transition income, buyouts, and retraining, but most would lose their established occupation; the dairy and hide workshop would close. Should the national government choose dry-forest restoration to protect the ebony’s genetic diversity or renew the licences to protect these livelihoods?

At the metropolitan fringe, a single-track passenger railway runs through a narrow state-owned gorge containing a continuous old-growth western redcedar–western hemlock ecosystem. Its mature canopy, hollow trees, nurse logs, deep organic soils, seepage-fed benches, and humid streamside conditions have developed through long ecological continuity. An environmental regulatory agency must set the boundary of a new strict protected area. Including the railway margins and the only feasible passing-track site would preserve the existing rail line and its maintenance footprint but bar the clearing, grading, retaining walls, and drainage works needed for a second track. The gorge would retain its continuous canopy, seepage-fed soils, deadwood, humid understory, and stream-corridor habitat without a new linear opening.

Excluding a 2.4-kilometer transport strip would allow a full-length passing track and dependable half-hourly passenger service. It would also remove about 4.6 hectares of old-growth forest, create a permanently widened illuminated corridor, cut old-tree roots and seepage paths, redirect groundwater from organic soils, and dry moisture-dependent communities beyond the cleared area. Residents of three commuter towns rely on the railway for work, education, medical appointments, shopping, and regional services. Without the passing track, trains remain roughly two-hourly, crowded, and prone to delays; an hourly bus remains available but is slower and lacks the same connections, leaving many round trips 45–80 minutes longer. Should the environmental regulatory agency choose protected-area designation that protects the old-growth ecosystem or exclude the transport strip to protect residents’ mobility?

A region-owned concrete dam in a tropical highland valley no longer produces hydropower, but its reservoir sustains a licensed cooperative fishery of introduced tilapia and small pelagic fish. Residents of six road-isolated towns, particularly low-income households, buy this inexpensive fresh fish several times a week. Imported meat, eggs, pulses, and canned fish cost substantially more, and rainy-season road closures make replacement deliveries less regular. If the regional government retains and maintains the dam, the cooperative can continue regular landings and roadside sales, preserving a stable, locally produced source of affordable food for ordinary meals.

Removing the dam would drain the reservoir and permanently end that fishery. Shops and freight services would still provide enough food to prevent hunger, but households would face enduring price increases, less frequent fresh-protein deliveries, and fewer foods affordable for routine meals. The restored river would not provide comparable harvests during the long recovery of native populations and would have far less commercial fishing area than the reservoir. Yet removal would reconnect headwaters, main-stem pools, and the floodplain: native migratory minnows and prawns could again reach their spawning, nursery, and dry-season refuge habitats. Their return would restore prey and nutrient transfers to native catfish, kingfishers, otters, and floodplain reptiles, while seasonal inundation would reconnect producer, detritivore, and consumer pathways across the river corridor.

Should the regional government remove the dam to protect trophic integrity or retain it to protect the towns’ affordable food access?

At the mouth of a monsoon river, forty-one lawful homes occupy a narrow distributary ridge. The neighborhood’s only access road and low ring levee cross all three tidal channels linking the river mouth to a mangrove-lined marine embayment. Those structures keep the house pads above ordinary spring tides and maintain road access, but they also constrict tidal flow. Inner creeks stagnate, dry-season hypersaline pockets form, and sediment, mangrove detritus, juvenile fish, and larger predators cannot move through the embayment as they once did. The resulting mangrove, mudflat, and shallow-water communities remain fragmented, with reduced nursery and benthic functions.

A river-basin authority can retain residential zoning, the road, and the levee, allowing residents to remain in their homes with their meeting hall, waterfront routines, and close mutual-aid relationships intact. Or it can adopt an eight-year residential phaseout, acquire the parcels, provide replacement homes in the nearby serviced town, and remove the road embankment and levee. That would reopen the distributary mouths and reconnect daily tides and seasonal river pulses, restoring salinity gradients, sediment and detritus transport, feeding grounds, fish passage, and predator access across the marine ecosystem. Relocation would be materially safeguarded, yet residents would permanently lose their present homes and established ridge community.

Should the river-basin authority choose the ecologically protective residential phaseout and restoration, or retain residential use to protect residents’ ability to remain in their community?

At a jointly owned floodplain on the boundary of three towns, a lowland meadow of native sedges, meadow-rue, burnet, floodplain orchids, and flood-tolerant grasses grows in moist alluvial soil. For more than a century, the towns’ midsummer processions have converged on this meadow for circle dances, a communal meal, music, and reciprocal hosting. The processions, dance circles, tents, and emergency-access lane occupy nearly all usable ground above the lowest flood swales. Annual footfall, dancing, tent installation, and access mats compact the moist soil, reducing the conditions needed for sensitive sedges, orchids, and floodplain forbs to recover. These plants are declining in the central footprint while trampling-tolerant grasses spread, simplifying the native plant community and leaving its diverse portions confined to narrow margins.

An intermunicipal public authority may designate the entire meadow as a protected area, prohibit the gathering and its required temporary works, remove the existing track base, and limit ordinary access to small groups on raised perimeter paths. The compacted areas would recover, allowing a continuous mixed sedge–forb–grass community to re-establish. Yet the three processions could no longer meet on their shared boundary ground, ending the place-specific dances, meal, hosting sequence, and intergenerational instruction in their established form. If the authority continues permitting the event, that cultural practice and the relationships it enacts will continue, but the meadow’s central native assemblage will progressively decline. Should the intermunicipal public authority choose protected-area designation to protect the native plant community or continue permitting the gathering to protect the cultural practice?
